usecase-low-carbon-heat/_overview.a: Heat decarbonization means reducing or removing carbon dioxide emissions from heat production and use. This can be achieved by using fuel in more efficient ways, e.g. by utilizing it for captive power generation (waste heat recovery). Carbon-free fuels could replace fossil fuel. Alternatively, you can electrify heat production by using power from renewable energy.

usecase-low-carbon-heat/_overview.q: What are the main benefits of decarbonizing process steam?
usecase-low-carbon-heat/_overview.a: Decarbonizing process steam significantly reduces greenhouse gas emissions, leading to a lower carbon footprint for industries. Additionally, it offers long-term energy cost savings and helps ensure compliance with regulatory standards aimed at promoting sustainability.

usecase-low-carbon-heat/_overview.q: What challenges do industries face when implementing waste heat recovery?
usecase-low-carbon-heat/_overview.a: Industries often encounter economic barriers related to initial investments and may struggle with integrating new technologies into existing systems without disrupting operations.

usecase-low-carbon-heat/_overview.q: Can hydrogen be used in existing heating systems?
usecase-low-carbon-heat/_overview.a: Yes, hydrogen can replace natural gas in many uses. For example the so-called green steel could be produced by replaing fossil fuels with hydrogen. However, changes may be needed based on the heating system's needs.

Waste heat recovery captures and reuses the heat generated by industrial processes that would otherwise get lost. This recovered heat can be used in other processes. It can also generate electricity. This helps improve energy efficiency and lowers overall energy costs.

usecase-organic-rankine-cycle/_overview.q: What is an Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) system?
usecase-organic-rankine-cycle/_overview.a: An Organic Rankine Cycle uses an organic fluid with a low boiling point instead of water/steam to convert low- to medium-temperature heat (typically 80 - 400°C) into electricity in a closed loop.

usecase-organic-rankine-cycle/_overview.q: How does ORC differ from a traditional steam turbine?
usecase-organic-rankine-cycle/_overview.a: ORC handles lower-temperature heat sources that steam turbines cannot efficiently use, employing organic fluids for vaporization at reduced pressures; steam turbines require higher temperatures (>400°C) and water/steam.

usecase-organic-rankine-cycle/_overview.q: What are typical ORC efficiency levels?
usecase-organic-rankine-cycle/_overview.a: ORC systems achieve 5–20% thermal efficiency depending on heat source temperature, lower than steam turbines (>40%) but valuable for recovering otherwise wasted low-grade heat.
ORC excels in waste heat recovery (industrial exhaust, cement/steel plants), geothermal power, biomass, solar thermal, and CHP/district heating.

usecase-organic-rankine-cycle/_overview.q: Can ORC systems operate without water?
usecase-organic-rankine-cycle/_overview.a: Yes, many ORC designs, including Siemens Energy's geothermal modules, are water-free using air cooling or dry fluids, ideal for water-scarce sites.

usecase-organic-rankine-cycle/_overview.q: What industries use ORC for waste heat recovery?
usecase-organic-rankine-cycle/_overview.a: Energy-intensive sectors like cement (up to 30% plant power), steel, glass, chemicals, and refineries recover flue gas/pre-heater heat to generate captive power and cut emissions.

usecase-organic-rankine-cycle/_overview.q: What temperature range suits ORC technology?
usecase-organic-rankine-cycle/_overview.a: ORC works best for low- to medium-grade heat: 80–400°C for waste heat/geothermal; Siemens small ORC handles 140–300°C circuits efficiently.

usecase-organic-rankine-cycle/_overview.q: What are ORC benefits for decarbonization?
usecase-organic-rankine-cycle/_overview.a: ORC recovers stranded heat, reducing fuel use/emissions by 10–30% in plants, supporting net-zero goals without process changes; enables CHP for district heating.

usecase-power-plant-resilience/_overview.q: What does operational resilience mean for power plant operators today?
usecase-power-plant-resilience/_overview.a: Operational resilience is the ability to maintain reliable, efficient, and flexible performance in the face of fluctuating demand, market changes, regulatory pressures, and unforeseen disruptions.

usecase-power-plant-resilience/_overview.q: Why is it important for operators to strengthen the operational resiliency of their gas-fired power plants?
usecase-power-plant-resilience/_overview.a: Operational resilience is the ability to maintain reliable, efficient, and flexible performance in the face of fluctuating demand, market changes, regulatory pressures, and unforeseen disruptions.

usecase-power-plant-resilience/_overview.q: What do power plant operators need to do to strengthen their operational resiliency?
usecase-power-plant-resilience/_overview.a: Strengthening operational resiliency requires a strategic evaluation of a plant's specific operational requirements and the prevailing market conditions. Operators must perform a comprehensive risk assessment to identify their most critical vulnerabilities and then align their resilience investments with their long-term commercial goals.

usecase-power-plant-resilience/_overview.q: What is the difference between power plant reliability and power plant resilience?
usecase-power-plant-resilience/_overview.a: Reliability refers to the plant’s ability to perform its intended function under normal operating conditions. Resilience, however, is the plant’s ability to withstand and adapt to changing market conditions and operational requirements.

usecase-power-plant-resilience/_overview.q: How does resilient gas-fired power plant support the energy transition?
usecase-power-plant-resilience/_overview.a: Resilient gas-fired power plants provide the essential flexibility and grid stability needed to balance intermittent renewables, ensuring a reliable power supply while transitioning toward carbon-neutral fuels like hydrogen.

usecase-storage-solutions/_overview.q: What is meant by energy storage?
usecase-storage-solutions/_overview.a: Energy storage refers to the process of capturing energy produced at one time for use at a later time. This is particularly important for balancing supply and demand, ensuring a stable and reliable energy supply, and integrating renewable energy sources like solar and wind, which can be intermittent. Energy storage works by converting energy from its original form into a storable form and then converting it back when needed.

usecase-storage-solutions/_overview.q: What types of energy storage technologies are commonly used?
usecase-storage-solutions/_overview.a: Battery Storage: Batteries store electrical energy in chemical form. When energy is needed, the chemical energy is converted back into electrical energy. This is useful for short-term storage and applications like grid stability and frequency regulation. Thermal Storage: This involves storing energy in the form of heat. For example, excess electricity can be used to heat a material (like molten salt), which can then be used to generate electricity later. Mechanical Storage: This includes methods like pumped hydro storage, where water is pumped to a higher elevation using excess electricity and then released to generate electricity when needed. Flywheels are another example, where rotational energy is stored and then converted back to electricity. Hydrogen Storage: Excess electricity can be used to produce hydrogen through electrolysis. The hydrogen can be stored and later used in fuel cells to generate electricity or for other applications.

usecase-storage-solutions/_overview.q: How do energy storage solutions contribute to a carbon-neutral energy future?
usecase-storage-solutions/_overview.a: Energy storage solutions play a critical role in the transition to a carbon-neutral energy future by enabling the integration of renewable energy sources like wind and solar into the power grid. They store surplus energy generated during periods of high production and release it during periods of high demand or low renewable energy availability, ensuring grid stability and reliability. By reducing the reliance on fossil-fuel-based power generation, energy storage supports decarbonization and helps create a sustainable energy ecosystem.

usecase-storage-solutions/_overview.q: What are the key benefits of using Siemens Energy’s storage solutions?

usecase-sustainable-fuels/_overview.q: What are sustainable gas turbine fuels?
usecase-sustainable-fuels/_overview.a: Sustainable gas turbine fuels are all fuels that produce very low or zero CO2 emissions, such as sustainable hydrogen (green, pink, blue, turquoise), its derivatives (e.g. e-ammonia, e-methanol) and 2nd generation biofuels, e.g. biogas, biomethane, hydrogenated vegetable oil (HVO), bio-methanol and bio-ethanol.

usecase-sustainable-fuels/_overview.q: What are the most effective alternative fuels for gas turbines compared to fossil fuels?
usecase-sustainable-fuels/_overview.a: All low or zero carbon fuels that fall within the fuel specification of the gas turbine model can significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions from gas power plants compared to fossil fuels. While blue hydrogen (and its derivatives) and biogenic fuels typically show 65-90% GHG emission reductions, green hydrogen and its derivatives can achieve 95-100% reductions.

usecase-sustainable-fuels/_overview.q: How can gas turbines achieve carbon neutrality or be decarbonized?
usecase-sustainable-fuels/_overview.a: Gas turbines can achieve carbon neutrality in two different ways: By using carbon neutral fuels (such as hydrogen, hydrogen derivatives or biofuels) or by using natural gas with carbon capture and storage (CCS).

usecase-sustainable-fuels/_overview.q: What is the optimal or most cost-effective alternative fuel for gas turbines?
usecase-sustainable-fuels/_overview.a: The most suitable sustainable fuel for a gas turbine depends on local factors such as the expected operating regime of the power plant, the availability and cost of alternative fuels, which vary widely from one region to another. The optimal fuel will therefore always be a project-specific decision.

usecase-sustainable-fuels/_overview.q: Is it currently possible to run a gas turbine on biogenic fuels?
usecase-sustainable-fuels/_overview.a: Several biogenic fuels have already been qualified for use in Siemens Energy gas turbines: While all frames can run on biomethane, there are first frames approved for use with HVO100 and bio-methanol. As development continues, more biogenic and other alternative fuels will become available for the Siemens Energy gas turbine product portfolio.
